recommended_fix: Swap the two groups: t1 = 14, mean_t1 = 161, se_t1 = 6, n_t1 = treatment n; t2 = 23, mean_t2 = 100, se_t2 = 8, n_t2 = control n (keep dose = 9). verifier_reasoning: Verified directly in the PDF. Methods p. 450-452: "The pregnant dam was housed at ambient temperature (Ta) of ~23 C... At day 1, the litter was assigned to one of two groups; Control litters continued to grow at the same ambient conditions, whereas the Cold litters were raised at 14 C from day 1 to 21. The cold exposure was obtained by placing the litter, with the dam, in a standard fridge." So 23 C = Control, 14 C = Cold treatment, unambiguously. Table 1 (p. 454) has columns Control then Cold: "UCP/wet tissue (% of Control) 100+/-8 | 161+/-6 | <0.001". The sheet holds mean_t1 = 100, se_t1 = 8, t1 = 23 (i.e. the Control column in the TREATMENT slot) and mean_t2 = 161, se_t2 = 6, t2 = 14 (the Cold column in the CONTROL slot). The mean_t1 = 100 value is itself decisive: the measure is expressed as "% of Control", so a mean of exactly 100 can only be the control group. Results 3.2 (p. 452) and the Abstract confirm the biological direction: "In Cold rats, the BAT total proteins, and, specifically, the UCP (Table 1) were substantially above the Control values." I also independently tested whether t1<t2 might be a sheet-wide convention rather than an error: across all 41 study files, t2 is consistently the repeated reference/control value and t1 the varying treatment, and cold-treatment-vs-warm-control rows are entered as t1<t2 in many studies (N17 14/22 and 17/22; WildNew6 10/20; s35 14/24; s39 -6/4; s44 15/28 and 20/28; s23 20/28; s53 20/30; s98 35/38; s59 literally 'high temperature'/'control'). N5 is the only file whose t2 is the treated group. Consequence, computed with the project's own effect size (R/1_data_process.R line 288 uses metafor escalc measure = "SMDH", then multiplies by -1 when mito_efficiency_dir == 0): as entered the row yields SMDH = -3.86, flipped to +3.86 by dir = 0, i.e. cold rearing appears to RAISE mitochondrial respiratory function; correctly entered it yields -1.93. The row's contribution is exactly sign-inverted.

claim: Developmental temperature was never experimentally manipulated or assigned in this study: all pups experienced an identical ambient thermal regime and the compared groups are post hoc behavioural categories, so the row does not meet inclusion criterion 1 and has no experimental control group (criterion 2).

paper_evidence: Methods, "Na+,K+-ATPase activities", p.1327: "Specific Na+,K+-ATPase activities at ambient temperature were measured at the water temperature to which each group had acclimated. The measurements at ambient temperatures are an estimation of the enzyme activity in vivo (specific activity at ambient temperature: SAamb)." So SAopt uses a single common 37C assay for every group (the baseline level of the assay-temperature factor) whereas SAamb uses 26C for the treatment group and 19C for the control group. verifier_reasoning: Verified independently in the PDF. Methods, 'Na+,K+-ATPase activities', p.1327: SAopt = 'Triplicate 5-ul aliquots of sucrose-buffer diluted homogenates were incubated for 15 min at the optimum temperature of 37 C'; SAamb = 'Specific Na+,K+-ATPase activities at ambient temperature were measured at the water temperature to which each group had acclimated. Here, incubation times were 20 min at 26 C, 30 min at 19 C and 45 min at 12 C.' Fig. 2 legend, p.1332 confirms the panel coding: 'Black bars indicate Na+,K+-ATPase activities in tissue homogenates incubated at the optimum assay temperature (SAopt) and grey bars those activities when tissue homogenates were incubated at the ambient temperature where each group acclimated (SAamb).' So SAopt is the common-assay (baseline) level of the assay-temperature factor and SAamb is not. Decisively, the authors themselves attribute the SAamb pattern to the assay temperature, not to any acclimation response - Discussion, 'Effects of ambient temperature', p.1333: 'The correlation between branchial Na+,K+-ATPase activities measured at ambient temperature (SAamb) and incubation temperature can then simply be explained from Arrhenius' law that describes the effect of temperature on reaction rate constants.' Two further points the first pass did not make: (i) the Results, p.1330 note that 'Acclimation to the highest temperature tested (26 C) only affected SAamb' in kidney, so the SAamb rows carry essentially all of this study's apparent temperature signal and it is thermodynamic, not biological; (ii) SAopt and SAamb were assayed on the SAME homogenates from the SAME fish, so kris_n_472/473 are not independent of kris_n_470/471 - sample_depend = 1 is set uniformly on all four rows, which is the right handling, but only if the downstream model treats that as one shared-animal cluster.

claim: Na+,K+-ATPase is a plasma-membrane ion pump, not a mitochondrial enzyme, so measurement_category "metabolic capacity" (the bin the project reserves for mitochondrial markers such as citrate synthase and cytochrome c oxidase) is wrong; these rows belong in "non-mitochondrial metabolic pathways".
paper_evidence: Introduction p.1326: "In osmoregulatory organs such as gills and kidney, the Na+,K+-ATPase pump is an important determinant of osmoregulatory capacity"; Methods p.1327 assays "the specific Na+- and K+-dependent, ouabain-sensitive ATPase activity" in whole gill-scraping and kidney homogenates (no mitochondrial isolation; mito_preparation is correctly left blank). The paper never measures respiration, coupling or any mitochondrial marker - Figs. 3 and 4 are iodothyronine deiodinases, Tables 2 and 3 are hormones and plasma metabolites. Ouabain-sensitive Na+,K+-ATPase is by definition basolateral plasma membrane, and is more clearly extra-mitochondrial than LDH, which the project rules already assign to "non-mitochondrial metabolic pathways".

recommended_fix: Recode measurement_category to "non-mitochondrial metabolic pathways" for all four rows. Because WildNew2 contributes nothing but ATPase, the recode determines whether this study enters the mitochondrial synthesis at all; it should not sit alongside CS/COX rows. mito_efficiency_dir = 1 is acceptable once the row is in the non-mitochondrial bin (higher activity = higher pumping capacity), but it is worth recording that higher Na+,K+-ATPase activity is an ATP *demand*, not a mitochondrial capacity.
verifier_reasoning: Verified independently. The assay is explicitly the plasma-membrane pump: Methods p.1327, 'The specific Na+- and K+-dependent, ouabain-sensitive ATPase activity was measured in triplicate in gill and kidney homogenates according to the method described by Flik et al. (1983)', on whole gill-arch scrapings and kidney homogenised in sucrose/EDTA/Tris buffer with no mitochondrial isolation or subcellular fractionation of any kind (so blank mito_preparation is correct). Introduction p.1326 frames it as an osmoregulatory transporter: 'In osmoregulatory organs such as gills and kidney, the Na+,K+-ATPase pump is an important determinant of osmoregulatory capacity (Marshall and Grosell 2005).' The Discussion p.1333 treats it as an ATP CONSUMER, not a mitochondrial capacity: 'The reduced ATP demand by decreased branchial Na+,K+-ATPase activities in vivo could result in a lower energy expenditure at low temperatures.' A full-text search for mitochond*, respirat*, oxygen consum*, citrate synth*, cytochrome, oxidative, antioxid*, catalase, superoxid* returns hits ONLY in the reference list (p.1334-1335) and one Introduction citation to another paper - the study itself measures nothing mitochondrial. Its other outcomes are iodothyronine deiodinases (Figs. 3-4), thyroid hormones (Table 3) and plasma metabolites/hormones (Table 2), none extracted. One nuance worth recording so nobody is misled later: gill Na+,K+-ATPase is enriched in 'mitochondria-rich cells' (a phrase that appears in a reference title on p.1335), but the enzyme itself is basolateral plasma membrane - the cell type is mitochondria-rich, the enzyme is not mitochondrial. I did NOT verify the first pass's side assertion that kris_n_491 (WildNew4) and merged_84 to merged_95 (s29) carry the same miscoding - those rows and PDFs are outside my scope and that part of the proposed fix should be checked by whoever audits those studies. mito_efficiency_dir = 1 is acceptable once the rows sit in the non-mitochondrial bin.

claim: The SD was back-calculated from the paper's SEM using n = 5 while the printed SEM is an N = 20 SEM, so sd_t1/sd_t2 are half the animal-level SD the paper implies; any standardised (SMD/Hedges g) effect size from this row will be about 2x too large.

All data are reported as means +/- 1 S.E.M." Table 1 footnote, p. 454: "Values are group means +/- 1 S.E.M. Number of animals was 20 in each group." Hence the animal-level SDs implied by Table 1 are 8*sqrt(20) = 35.8 and 6*sqrt(20) = 26.8 (% of control).
sheet_value: n_t1 = n_t2 = 5 with sd_t1 = 17.8885 = 8*sqrt(5) and sd_t2 = 13.4164 = 6*sqrt(5); the extractor note states n = 5 litters was chosen deliberately to avoid pseudoreplication.
recommended_fix: Make the SD and n mutually consistent. Either (a) keep the paper's basis: n = 20, sd = 35.78 and 26.83; or (b) keep the conservative litter-level n = 5 but state explicitly that the printed SEM is being treated as the litter-level SEM (which is what sd = se*sqrt(5) assumes) and, if the analysis uses SMD, note that this halves the pooled SD relative to the paper. For lnRR the two options are equivalent (sd^2/n = se^2 either way), so if the meta-analysis is lnRR-based this is a documentation fix; if SMD is computed anywhere, option (a) or an explicit sensitivity check is needed.
verifier_reasoning: Verified numerically and against the paper. Methods 2.5 (p. 452): "We used five litters per group, each litter with six animals. Then, measurements were performed on four animals/litter, chosen randomly among the six, for a total of N=20 per group. All data are reported as means +/- 1 S.E.M." The Table 1 footnote (p. 454) repeats it: "Values are group means +/- 1 S.E.M. Number of animals was 20 in each group." The sheet's sd values are exactly se*sqrt(5) (8*sqrt(5) = 17.888544 = sd_t1; 6*sqrt(5) = 13.416408 = sd_t2), while the SEM printed in Table 1 is an N = 20 SEM, so the animal-level SDs are 8*sqrt(20) = 35.777 and 6*sqrt(20) = 26.833 - exactly 2x the sheet values, as the first pass states. I upgrade the severity from medium to high on one point the first pass left conditional: it hedged that "if the meta-analysis is lnRR-based this is a documentation fix", but the project is NOT lnRR-based. R/1_data_process.R line 288 computes metafor::escalc(measure = "SMDH", ...) with an explicit comment rejecting lnRR ("The data contain ratios (RCR, relative expression), percentages, zeros and skewed measurement variables, all of which complicate lnRR"). So the mismatch is fully load-bearing, not documentation: with the groups swapped back, n = 5 gives SMDH = 3.858 (v = 1.503, SE = 1.23) whereas n = 20 gives SMDH = 1.929 (v = 0.158, SE = 0.40). The row is therefore simultaneously an extreme magnitude outlier (2x) and ~9.5x less precise than the paper supports, so it is both over-stated and badly weighted. The extractor's pseudoreplication concern is legitimate in principle (temperature was assigned at the litter level - "At day 1, the litter was assigned to one of two groups"), but pairing a between-animal SEM with a litter-level n is the wrong way to implement it, because sd = se*sqrt(5) silently doubles the effect size instead of down-weighting it.

R1028) treats it purely as a contractile property: "Hydrolysis of ATP by myosin ATPase activity drives the cycle of interaction between actin and myosin", and the paper's own framing separates it from the "metabolic capacities" (LDH, COX): "Neither aerobic nor anaerobic metabolic capacities were directly linked to changes in muscle performance" (Abstract). claim: This is a 3-week thermal ACCLIMATION of large juveniles (69 g), not a manipulation over an early developmental window, and the paper gives no age - so criterion 1 ('during development, before sexual maturity') is met only on a literal reading and the row set sits at the permissive edge of the review's scope.
